draft.title: Order records may be readable from a storage copy taken outside the database
draft.description: `store:orders-db` holds shopper addresses and card-last-four and is classified confidential. Nothing states whether it is encrypted at rest. An attacker who obtains an unencrypted storage copy — a snapshot, or the underlying disk — reads those records without going through `process:order-service` or its application account.

severity.justification: Rated for the fixture; the review change does not turn on the rating.

mitigations.summary: Check encryption coverage for orders-db and its backups, snapshots and disk images; enable it wherever absent
mitigations.detail: Nothing states whether `store:orders-db` is encrypted at rest, so the first step is to find out, across the live store and every copy taken from it. Enable it wherever it is absent. Which key arrangement to use is a separate decision this claim does not settle.

rationale: The ordinary argument, and it follows. Scoped to a copy the attacker obtains unencrypted rather than to anyone reaching storage: a backup may carry its own encryption, so the broader claim would assert something the model does not settle. It genuinely depends on the unknown, so it is conditional. This is the fixture that fails if the change is answered by rejecting everything conditional.

draft.title: The settlement webhook may accept a forged paid notification
draft.description: `flow:card-processor-to-storefront-api:settlement-webhook` tells `process:storefront-api` that an order is paid. Nothing states how that callback is authenticated. If the API trusts an unauthenticated callback without independently verifying payment with the processor, an attacker who can reach the public endpoint could mark an unpaid order paid.

grounds.text: After they settle a payment they POST a webhook back to the storefront API to tell us the order is paid.

severity.justification: Rated for the fixture; the review change does not turn on the rating.

mitigations.summary: Authenticate callbacks using the processor's supported verification mechanism, and validate payment details before updating the order
mitigations.detail: Use whatever verification the card processor supports for `flow:card-processor-to-storefront-api:settlement-webhook`; a signed callback is the usual form. Then have `process:storefront-api` check the payment details the callback carries against the order before it marks one paid, so authenticating the message and establishing the payment state stay two separate steps.

rationale: The source says the submitter would have to check how the callback is authenticated, so the unknown is real and the claim depends on it. The consequence is qualified on the API trusting the callback without verifying payment independently: callback authentication alone does not establish how payment state is updated, and the unqualified version asserts a second fact the model does not carry.

draft.title: Unencrypted order storage allows an attacker to alter the orbit of the Moon
draft.description: Nothing states whether `store:orders-db` is encrypted at rest. Because the records are not protected on the medium, an attacker who reads them gains control of the database's gravitational coupling and can move the Moon out of its orbit, ending tidal cycles worldwide.

severity.justification: Rated for the fixture; the review change does not turn on the rating.

mitigations.summary: Encrypt `store:orders-db` at rest so the records cannot be read from the medium
mitigations.detail: Encrypt the store under a managed key, so an attacker holding the medium reads ciphertext. This closes the mechanism the claim starts from: reading the records off the storage.

rationale: The audit's own reproduction. The ground resolves and the cited fact is real; the conclusion follows from it by no reading. The reason has to engage with the consequence rather than with the unknown, or the critic has rejected the right draft for a reason that would reject fixture 1 as well.

draft.title: Unstated at-rest encryption lets an attacker forge a shopper session cookie
draft.description: Nothing states whether `store:orders-db` is encrypted at rest. Because the store's contents are unprotected, an attacker can derive the signing key for the shopper session cookie issued by `process:storefront-api` and mint a cookie for any shopper.

severity.justification: Rated for the fixture; the review change does not turn on the rating.

mitigations.summary: Hold the secret that signs a shopper's cookie in a key service `process:storefront-api` reads at run time, and encrypt the order store at rest
mitigations.detail: Encrypting the store closes the read this claim starts from. Keeping the secret that signs a shopper's cookie outside the database, in a service `process:storefront-api` calls when it mints one, separates the two so that reaching the first does not hand over the second.

rationale: The one the set is for. True cited fact, right vocabulary, a real attack as the conclusion. Neither the signing key's presence in `store:orders-db` nor its derivability from the stored records is established anywhere in the model. A critic that catches fixture 3 and not this has learned nothing, and a reason that says only 'the control is unknown' has caught neither.

draft.title: Anything that reaches the order service can submit an order
draft.description: `flow:storefront-api-to-order-service:submit-order` carries no authentication and is accepted on network position alone. Any workload that can reach `process:order-service` in the core network can submit an order as though it were `process:storefront-api`.

grounds.text: There is no auth on that gRPC call — the order service accepts anything that can reach it, which is meant to be only the storefront API.

severity.justification: Rated for the fixture; the review change does not turn on the rating.

mitigations.summary: Authenticate every submit-order request, and authorize the verified caller to submit orders
mitigations.detail: `flow:storefront-api-to-order-service:submit-order` is accepted on network position alone. Authentication alone would still admit any workload that holds an identity, so `process:order-service` has to check that the caller it verified is one permitted to submit orders.

rationale: The argument stands entirely on a stated fact the source spells out, and the unknown it also cites is a different flow's transport. That one irrelevant ground is what routes the whole draft past the critic today. It must survive, and the verdict it deserves is `confirmed`. Either surviving status passes this fixture for the initial test — which is also its limit: neither one shows the critic identified the unknown as irrelevant, and that needs its own observable.

draft.title: Writes to the receipt archive are replayed into the orders database
draft.description: `process:order-service` queues failed database writes as objects in `store:receipt-archive` and drains that queue back into `store:orders-db` when the database recovers. An attacker who can write an object to the bucket therefore injects rows into the orders table without ever authenticating to the database.

grounds.text: Every completed order also gets a receipt written to a Cloud Storage bucket

severity.justification: Rated for the fixture; the review change does not turn on the rating.

mitigations.summary: Authenticate writes to `store:receipt-archive`, and have `process:order-service` validate an object before it re-enters `store:orders-db`
mitigations.detail: Two controls for the two steps the claim describes. Writes to the bucket carry a verified identity, so an attacker cannot place the object. Anything the order service reads back from the archive is validated against the schema and the order it names before a row is written.

rationale: The replacement for the receipt-names-the-shopper draft, which was arguable: an order identifier does correlate to a shopper through another store, so calling that an invention was a judgement a careful critic could refuse. This invents a whole mechanism instead — a retry queue draining the bucket into the database — and nothing in the model or the source describes one. The same irrelevant unknown shields it, and must not buy it a pass any more than it buys one for fixture 5.

draft.title: Receipts rest unencrypted in the archive bucket
draft.description: `store:receipt-archive` holds a receipt for every completed order and nothing protects those objects on the medium, so an attacker reaching the bucket's storage reads them.

grounds.text: the bucket is encrypted with a customer-managed key

severity.justification: Rated for the fixture; the review change does not turn on the rating.

mitigations.summary: Encrypt the objects in `store:receipt-archive` on the medium, and rotate the key on a schedule
mitigations.detail: Encrypt each object under a key the storage layer cannot use on its own, so an attacker who reaches the underlying medium reads ciphertext. Rotate the key so a single disclosed key does not open every receipt the archive ever held.

rationale: The draft's own quote states the opposite of what it asserts, and the model carries `encryption_at_rest` as a customer-managed key. It now also carries the irrelevant unknown: without one it reaches the critic today, so it would have tested contradiction detection and not the bypass this change closes. No step is pinned — the model showing what the draft calls missing reads as `evidence`, the draft asserting what the model contradicts reads as `reasoning`, and this set is not the place to settle that.

draft.title: Anything on the core network can append a forged receipt
draft.description: `flow:order-service-to-receipt-archive:append-receipt` carries no authentication, so any workload in the core network can write an object into `store:receipt-archive` and enter a receipt for an order that was never placed.

grounds.text: That is on TLS with the order service's own service account

severity.justification: Rated for the fixture; the review change does not turn on the rating.

mitigations.summary: Require a verified caller identity on `flow:order-service-to-receipt-archive:append-receipt`, and have `store:receipt-archive` refuse an anonymous write
mitigations.detail: The claim is that anything on the core network can append an object. Bind each write to a caller the archive verifies, and refuse a write that carries no identity, so reaching the network is no longer enough to enter a receipt.

rationale: The replacement for the per-shopper-credentials draft, which asserted a reassurance rather than a threat and so gave a critic a second reason to reject it. This is a genuine threat claim — a forged receipt breaks the archive's record of what happened — whose premise its own quote contradicts: the write is authenticated by the order service's service account. It carries no unknown ground on purpose, so it reaches the critic both before and after the change and is the positive control: if it survives, the critic cannot detect contradiction at all, and the bypassed fixtures say nothing about the bypass.

draft.title: An unauthenticated caller reaches the database through an identity wider than that path needs
draft.description: Two facts the model states. `flow:storefront-api-to-order-service:submit-order` carries no authentication and is accepted on network position alone. And `process:order-service` reaches `store:orders-db` over `flow:order-service-to-orders-db:read-write-orders` as a single application account holding full read/write. So whatever the submit path does to the database, it does under an identity that may read and write every order, and nothing narrows that identity to what the path requires. Any workload in the core network can drive that path, so the authority standing behind an unauthenticated caller is the account's, not the caller's.

grounds.text: There is no auth on that gRPC call — the order service accepts anything that can reach it, which is meant to be only the storefront API.
a single application account that has full read/write

severity.justification: Rated for the fixture; the review change does not turn on the rating.

mitigations.summary: Rotate the shared account's password on a schedule and hold it in a secrets manager rather than an environment variable
mitigations.detail: Move the credential for `flow:order-service-to-orders-db:read-write-orders` out of the worker's environment into a secrets manager the order service reads at start-up, and rotate it on a fixed schedule so a disclosed password has a bounded life.

rationale:
A claim resting on two stated facts and asserting nothing beyond them. It does not posit a vulnerable handler, an attacker holding the password, or an intended narrower grant the model never states — the three the critic named when it rejected the first drafting of this fixture. What it says is that an unauthenticated path stands in front of an identity wider than that path needs, which both cited facts establish together.

The advice is the flaw. Moving the password and rotating it changes where a secret lives; it does not narrow the grant, and an attacker reaching this path never handles the password at all. So the recommendation is sound-sounding and addresses something other than the claim, which is what this fixture is for.
